summary: Specifies the frame format for encapsulating an IPv6 datagram in a MAPOS frame, and how an IPv6 interface identifier is formed on such links. MAPOS is a link-layer protocol for multiple access over SONET/SDH. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3572 specifies how to carry IPv6 datagrams over MAPOS links. It defines the frame value for IPv6, how destination addresses map to link addresses, and how nodes form and check IPv6 interface identifiers.

questions: how is ipv6 carried over mapos
what is the mapos mtu for ipv6
how are ipv6 interface identifiers formed on mapos
subtitle: Frame and address rules for carrying IPv6 datagrams over MAPOS links.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs link-layer rules for sending datagrams over MAPOS, a multiple-access protocol for SONET/SDH links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the IPv6 frame protocol value, address mapping, interface identifier creation, duplicate address detection and Neighbor Discovery link-layer address options.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3572 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 3572 is an Informational RFC and was updated by RFC 8064. The RFC states that it is not a standards-track document or a product of an IETF working group.

sections.title: IPv6 on a MAPOS Link
sections.content:
MAPOS is a link-layer protocol that provides multiple access over SONET/SDH. A frame switch can connect hosts and routers in a star-shaped LAN, including across long-haul links.

This memo specifies how IPv6 datagrams fit in MAPOS frames, how to form interface identifiers and detect duplicates, and how to format the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS carries frames between devices connected through a frame switch. This memo gives IPv6 the rules it needs to use that link.

sections.title: Frame Format and Maximum Size
sections.content:
A MAPOS frame uses HDLC-like framing. Its header includes address, control and protocol fields; MAPOS 16 uses a 16-bit address field and omits the version 1 control field. The IPv6 protocol field is 0x0057, and the information field contains the IPv6 header followed by its payload.

The information field must not exceed 65,280 octets. This is also the default MTU, though a Router Advertisement or manual configuration may set a lower value.
sections.plainLanguage: The frame's protocol field tells the receiver that its contents are IPv6. The frame can carry up to 65,280 octets of information, unless the configured MTU is lower.

sections.title: Mapping Unicast and Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
For unicast traffic, the MAPOS frame carries the destination interface's HDLC address, assigned through the Node Switch Protocol. IPv6 Neighbor Discovery resolves the destination link-layer address.

For multicast, the frame address is formed from the low-order bits of the IPv6 multicast address plus MAPOS-specific indicator bits. The exact field layout differs between MAPOS version 1 and MAPOS 16, and the RFC defines special values for cases where those low-order bits are all zero or all one.
sections.plainLanguage: For a single destination, Neighbor Discovery finds the destination's MAPOS link address. For multicast, the sender places selected bits of the IPv6 group address into the MAPOS address field.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Duplicate Detection
sections.content:
A node with MAPOS interfaces must create EUI-64-based IPv6 interface identifiers and must not derive them from MAPOS addresses. A MAPOS address may depend on the switch and port, may not be globally unique, and can change when a connection changes.

The RFC prefers an IEEE global identifier if one is available. Otherwise, it suggests another unique source, such as a machine serial number, or a random value. After the MAPOS address is assigned, the node must run duplicate address detection on its unicast addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A MAPOS address can change when an interface moves, so it should not be used to create the IPv6 interface identifier. Once the link address is assigned, the node checks that its unicast IPv6 addresses are not duplicates.

sections.title: Security Limits of MAPOS
sections.content:
MAPOS has no link-layer security. A frame-switch-assigned address can help locate an interface, but a MAPOS frame has no sender-address field, which makes it difficult to identify the source of improper traffic.

The RFC suggests keeping multi-switch environments small, separating them with IP routers, and filtering traffic at boundary routers. It also notes there is no protection against accidental or forged duplicate interface identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS does not authenticate or encrypt traffic at the link layer. Routers can limit the reach of a MAPOS network, but duplicate IPv6 interface identifiers remain a risk described by the RFC.
